new_statements.quote: The rules of stress assignment that account for many phonological words in Anamuxra may be summarised as follows: (R-11) assign stress to a final heavy syllable where heavy syllable equals VV or VC; if there no final heavy syllable, assign stress to the penultimate syllable⁶. [fn. 6: In other words, "stress syllable containing penultimate mora".] ... Stress associates with underlying vowels wherever possible. Thus, 'target' syllables (i.e. penultimate and final heavy syllables) which contain an epenthetic vowel at surface level are not immediately available to the rules of stress assignment. Rather, stress is assigned to the nearest syllable to the left containing an underlying vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel/diphthong VV or closed VC), otherwise on the penult — equivalently, on the syllable containing the penultimate mora. Epenthetic vowels cannot bear stress: if the target syllable has an epenthetic vowel, stress goes to the nearest syllable to its left with an underlying vowel (or to the right if none exists to the left). Examples: [aβáβ] 'mother's brother', [arambaŋgín] 'four days hence' (final heavy) vs [árpʌ] 'tree-CL', [βuɣasírpʌ] 'spider-CL', [ʌpapurápʌ] 'butterfly-CL' (penult).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the thesis speaks only of a single primary stress per phonological word (compounds, noun+article/demonstrative, serialised verbs and bound pronominals form one phonological word with one primary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Author says the rule accounts for 'many' (not all) phonological words. Explicit exception: verbs inflected for near tense with 3sg subject take antepenultimate stress ([dáriya] 'hear-NT-3SGS', [támiya], [tór iya]) versus regular [darína] 'hear-NT-2SGS', [torín] 'hold-NT-1SGS' — 'clearly morphologically driven'. Epenthetic-vowel syllables are skipped ([índəpa] 'fishing spear-CL', [mátɨkəpa] 'crocodile-CL', [səɣʌ́] 'again').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem plus classifier/inflectional suffixes and incorporated bound forms); examples are citation forms of inflected words. Description based mainly on the Waiateng ('southern') dialect where Ingram did most fieldwork, with data also from Ikundun and Mindivi; no dialect differences in stress are mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Ingram's 'Anamuxra' = Glottolog anam1248 / ISO imi, the language earlier called Ikundun (Z'graggen) in the Josephstaal (Pomoikan) group; Ingram distinguishes a northern dialect (Mindivi, Ikundun, Tuamadapuar) and a southern dialect (Apovd, Swanzambi, Waiateng); his data come chiefly from Waiateng (southern) with some Ikundun and Mindivi material. No stress differences between dialects are reported.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.5 'Stress' (pp. 51-53): rule (R-11) stress a final heavy syllable (VV or VC), otherwise the penult (fn. 6: 'stress syllable containing penultimate mora'); stress skips epenthetic vowels (shifts to nearest underlying vowel to the left, else right); morphologically driven exception: near-tense 3sg-subject verbs take antepenultimate stress. Elsewhere (ch. 5, 6, SVC chapter) compounds/bound pronouns/serial verbs form one phonological word with a single primary stress.
